title: Flexible mechanisms

definition.text: The three Kyoto Protocol tools, emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation, that let countries meet emission targets more cheaply by acting in other countries.

facts.text: They rest on the idea that cutting emissions costs different amounts in different places, but benefits the atmosphere equally wherever it happens.
International emissions trading let parties buy Kyoto units from other countries to help meet their targets.
Kyoto caps required Annex I countries to cut emissions on average 5.2% below 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012.
The main argument for them is cost-effectiveness, separating fairness from the efficiency of cutting emissions cheaply.
Critics feared rich countries would avoid domestic cuts and take up all the cheap reductions in developing countries.
Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement are their successor.

contested_note: Negotiators disagreed over whether flexibility was efficient or let developed countries avoid domestic cuts at developing countries' expense.

definition.text: A tradable certificate proving that a certain amount of electricity, typically one megawatthour, was generated from renewable sources.

facts.text: The certificates represent the environmental value of renewable energy and can be traded separately from the electricity itself.
Countries such as Poland, Sweden, the UK, Italy and Belgium use them as a more market-like alternative to feed-in tariffs.
Buying one only shifts the claim to renewable power; it does not change how much renewable energy is generated.

definition.text: A Kyoto Protocol mechanism letting one developed (Annex I) country invest in an emission-cutting project in another and count the cuts towards its own target.

facts.text: Projects earn Emission Reduction Units, each equal to one tonne of CO2 equivalent, taken from the host country's pool of assigned amount units.
Because credits come from the host's pool, the total of credits among Annex I parties does not change.
It raised fewer concerns about spurious reductions than the CDM, since hosts also have emission commitments.
Russia accounted for about two-thirds of projected savings, which were expected to total around 300 million ERUs by 2012.

title: Market design

definition.text: The branch of economics that sets the rules of exchange, who gets what and by what procedure, to build or repair markets so that they give efficient and fair outcomes.

facts.text: It is closely related to mechanism design and auction theory.
Applications pioneered by Alvin Roth include labour-market matching, organ transplantation and school choice.
Under the revenue equivalence theorem, expected revenue is the same in sealed first-price and second-price auctions with independent private values.
Roth and Shapley won the 2012 Nobel prize for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design.
